did_you_know.text: After Joshua’s death, the Israelites do not act on their own initiative. Instead, they ask the Lord who should be the first to go up and fight the Canaanites.
Judah invites his brother Simeon to join him, promising to return the favor and help him in his allotted territory.
At the battle of Bezek, Judah and Simeon defeat the Canaanites and Perizzites, and the text states that ten thousand men were killed.
Adoni-bezek describes punishment as measure for measure: after humiliating seventy kings, he himself is humiliated in a similar way and recognizes it as repayment from God.
Caleb offers his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever captures Kiriath-sepher, linking the conquest with the establishment of a family.
Achsah asks not only for the Negev land she received but also for sources of water. Caleb grants her the upper and lower springs.
After Zephath is captured and placed under the ban, the city is named Hormah. The name is explicitly connected with the act of placing it under the ban described in the verse.
The chapter presents both success and limitation: Judah dispossesses the inhabitants of the hill country but cannot dispossess those in the valley because the Canaanites had iron chariots.
The Benjamites did not dispossess the Jebusites living in Jerusalem, and the text says that the Jebusites continued to live there alongside them.

The chapter lists several tribes that did not dispossess all the inhabitants of the land within their allotted territories. In some places, the Canaanites remained and became forced laborers; in others, they continued to live among the Israelites.
